name: com.kibootia.backend.academic
comment: Academic module: the roles, permissions and per-record authorization rules of Timetia (Timetia ADR 0004). It holds no timetable or ticket data. The modules that own those implement the facts interfaces in this package and ask the decision point about their records; this module only decides who may.

name: com.kibootia.backend.academic.AcademicConfiguration
comment: Wires the academic rules into the decision point and declares the kinds of place Timetia roles apply to.

name: com.kibootia.backend.academic.AcademicPermissions
comment:
The permissions of Timetia's lecture rescheduling and live timetable, as the role and scope model document lists them (Timetia ADR 0004). All but three are policy-decided: they are held through a role assigned within a scope, and decided per record by {@link com.kibootia.backend.academic.domain.AcademicAccessPolicy}. The three flat ones are for Super Admin, the built-in Administrator, which holds every flat permission and no policy-decided one.

The names are stored in role definitions, so when the ticket and timetable modules exist their owners can take over these declarations without renaming anything.

name: com.kibootia.backend.academic.AcademicScopes
comment: The kinds of place a Timetia role can be assigned in. {@code GLOBAL} is the platform's own and is not listed.

name: com.kibootia.backend.academic.IssueAccessFacts
comment: What the policy needs to know about an issue a CR or BR opened about a lecture.

methods.name: mentionedFacultyUserIds
methods.comment: The faculty mentioned on the issue, as user ids.

name: com.kibootia.backend.academic.LectureAccessFacts
comment: What the policy needs to know about a lecture, an occurrence of one or a record about one. The module that owns the record passes an implementation to {@code Authorization.require(action, facts)}; this module reads it and never changes it. People are user ids, resolved by the module that owns them. A missing value never grants anything.

methods.name: departmentId
methods.comment: The department of the lecture's division.

methods.name: batchIds
methods.comment: Every batch the lecture is for. A theory lecture of a division lists all batches of that division, and a shared course lists the batches of every division that takes it.

methods.name: teachingFacultyUserIds
methods.comment: The faculty who teach the lecture, as user ids.

name: com.kibootia.backend.academic.SessionType
comment: The kind of a lecture: theory, or a lab or tutorial session. CR and BR rights depend on it.

name: com.kibootia.backend.academic.TicketAccessFacts
comment: What the policy needs to know about a ticket: the lecture it concerns and the people on it.

methods.name: authorUserId
methods.comment: The author, whether a faculty member or an HOD acting for one.

methods.name: affectedFacultyUserIds
methods.comment: The faculty affected by the change, as user ids.

methods.name: requestedReviewerUserIds
methods.comment: The people asked to review, as user ids.

methods.name: permanentChange
methods.comment: Whether the change is permanent. A permanent change is reverted only by an HOD or Super HOD.

name: com.kibootia.backend.academic.application.RoleTemplateSeeder
comment: Creates the Timetia roles at startup in the default tenant (Timetia ADR 0004). A role that already exists is left alone, so an administrator's edits to a seeded role are never undone; a permission added to a template later reaches a role that already exists only when an administrator adds it.

methods.name: seed
methods.comment: Creates the roles that are missing and returns how many it created. Safe to repeat.

name: com.kibootia.backend.academic.domain.AcademicAccessPolicy
comment:
The rules of the role and scope model, one per permission (Timetia ADR 0004). It is called only when the caller holds the permission in at least one place, and it can only narrow that: a rule that does not match answers no.

A permission is either relation-based (the caller must be one of the named people on the record), scope-based (a grant must cover the record) or both. {@link #covers} says when a grant covers a lecture:

  • a global grant covers every lecture;
  • a department grant covers a lecture of that department;
  • a division grant covers a lecture of that division, and a batch grant a lecture that lists the batch;
  • for the actions that CR and BR perform, a division grant applies to theory lectures only and a batch grant to lab and tutorial lectures only. Department and global grants have no such limit.

A missing id, set or session type in the facts never matches. An action this policy does not know is denied. No permission lets anyone override a conflict, so none appears here: that is a rule of the ticket module.

methods.name: covers
methods.comment: Whether one of the grants covers the lecture. With {@code sessionRule}, a division grant needs a theory lecture and a batch grant a lab or tutorial lecture.

name: com.kibootia.backend.academic.domain.AcademicRoles
comment: The role templates of the role and scope model (Timetia ADR 0004): a name, the kind of place it is assigned in and the permissions it carries. Super Admin is not here: it is the built-in Administrator role.

name: com.kibootia.backend.academic.domain.AcademicRoles$Template
comment: One role to seed.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access
comment: Access module. See kibootia-docs/engineering/conventions/package-structure.md.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.AccessConfiguration
comment: Wires the decision point (ADR 0044): the permissions every module declares and the Java policies. A caller's permissions come from the stored roles ({@code StoredPermissionSource}, found by component scanning).

methods.name: scopeKinds
methods.comment: {@code GLOBAL} and the kinds of place modules declare (Timetia ADR 0004).

methods.name: requiredPermissionsAreDeclared
methods.comment: Every {@code @RequiresPermission} must name a declared permission, and not a policy-decided one: a typo stops the application at startup, and so does a permission that only a record check can satisfy (Timetia ADR 0004).

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.AccessPermissions
comment: The permissions of the access module (ADR 0044). None is held by the built-in {@code user} role; the administrator role holds every permission.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.RoleAssignments
comment:
What the {@code identity} module needs from {@code access} when it manages an account's life (ADR 0039, ADR 0041). The module's own screens use the use cases behind {@code /api/v1/roles}; this contract is for the steps of the user lifecycle, which {@code identity} has already authorized.

Methods that write need the caller's transaction ({@code MANDATORY}), so a role change and the user change it belongs to commit or roll back together.

methods.name: permissionsOf
methods.comment: Every permission the user holds through their roles; for the administrator role, every declared flat permission. A policy-decided permission held in any place is included, as a hint for the interface: a decision about a record is made by the decision point, never from this list.

methods.name: rolesOf
methods.comment: The user's roles, built-in ones first.

methods.name: rolesOf
methods.comment: The roles of several users at once, for a list screen. A user with no role is absent from the map.

methods.name: holdsAdministratorRole
methods.comment: Whether the user holds the built-in administrator role.

methods.name: assignDefaultRole
methods.comment: Gives a new profile the built-in {@code user} role. Does nothing when the user already holds it.

methods.name: assignInitialRoles
methods.comment: Gives an invited user the roles the inviting administrator chose, after the default one. The caller needs permission to assign roles, and the administrator role may only be given by an administrator.

methods.name: grantFirstAdministrator
methods.comment: Makes the user an administrator when no administrator exists. Returns whether it did. The caller has already checked the bootstrap setting and the user's verified email address.

methods.name: hasAdministrator
methods.comment: Whether anyone holds the administrator role, signed in or not. It tells startup whether the bootstrap administrator is still needed (Timetia ADR 0006).

methods.name: ensureNotLastAdministrator
methods.comment: Refuses with 409 {@code access.last_administrator} when the user is an administrator and the only one who can still sign in. It locks the administrator role, so two administrators cannot remove each other at once. The calling transaction must use {@code READ_COMMITTED}, so the count sees what a concurrent commit changed.

methods.name: removeAll
methods.comment: Removes every role from the user, when the user is erased.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.RoleSummary
comment: A role as other modules see it: enough to show which roles a user holds.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.RoleTemplates
comment: What a module needs from {@code access} to seed the roles of its own domain at startup (Timetia ADR 0004), for example the Timetia roles. Called with the tenant bound and in a transaction, before any user is signed in.

methods.name: ensure
methods.comment: Creates the role when no live role has this name, and never changes one that exists, so an administrator's edits to a seeded role stay. A permission that no module declares any more is left out.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.ScopedAssignments
comment:
What a module that loads people in bulk (Timetia's provisioning import) needs from {@code access} to give roles within a scope: turn the names a file uses into a role and a place, and add the assignment when it is missing. Both are for administrators only and check that themselves, and neither can reach a platform role: only a role with a scope type is ever found by name (Timetia ADR 0006).

This only ever adds. Taking an assignment away is the administrator's screen, one person at a time.

methods.name: resolve
methods.comment: Finds the role by its exact name and the place by its code, applying every rule an assignment must meet: the role has a scope type; a {@code GLOBAL} role takes no place; every other needs one, and it must exist. Never throws for a bad row; the refusal is in the result. Nothing is written.

methods.name: addIfMissing
methods.comment: Gives the user the resolved role in the resolved place unless they already hold it there, auditing a new assignment with the role, the scope type and the place. Returns whether it added one; {@code false} means it was already held, and nothing changed. Re-checks the role and the place itself, so it does not trust a stale or forged resolution. Runs in the caller's transaction, so the assignment commits or rolls back with what the caller is doing.  @throws com.kibootia.backend.platform.errors.ApiException 404 when the user does not exist, 400 when the role or place is no longer valid

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.ScopedAssignments$Failure
comment: Why a row cannot be assigned. The names are the {@code code} the import reports.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.ScopedAssignments$Resolution
comment: Either a role and place ready to assign ({@link #failure} is null), or the reason a row cannot be assigned, as a code from {@link Failure} and a message for the person preparing the file.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.application.BuiltInRoles
comment: The administrator and user roles (ADR 0025, ADR 0041). They are created at startup in the default tenant, and the user role is offered every permission a module flags for it that it has not seen yet, once, so an administrator's removals stay removed. Use cases that need one of them call {@link #admin()} or {@link #user()}, which create it first if it is missing, so a database that lost the rows heals itself instead of refusing every sign-in.

methods.name: run
methods.comment: Startup: the tenant is bound before the transaction starts, because Hibernate reads it when a session opens.

methods.name: admin
methods.comment: In the caller's transaction and tenant.

methods.name: user
methods.comment: In the caller's transaction and tenant.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.application.NewRole
comment: What an administrator supplies to create a role.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.application.Role
comment: A role as the use cases see it, apart from the table row and the API type (ADR 0004).

methods.name: isScoped
methods.comment: Whether the role carries policy-decided permissions and so is assigned within a scope.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.application.Role$BuiltIn
comment: The roles the foundation creates and protects.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.application.RoleAssignmentService
comment:
Who holds which role (ADR 0025, ADR 0041). It serves the role screens of the administration interface and, through {@link RoleAssignments}, the steps of the user lifecycle that {@code identity} drives.

The safeguards live here because this module owns the assignments: the administrator role is only given by an administrator, and the last administrator who can still sign in cannot be removed ({@link #ensureNotLastAdministrator}).

methods.name: rolesOfUser
methods.comment: The roles a user holds.

methods.name: replaceRolesOfUser
methods.comment:
Makes the user's roles exactly {@code roleIds}. The administrator role can only be given by an administrator, and taking it from the last active administrator is refused. Every added and removed role is audited.

READ_COMMITTED so the last-administrator count sees what a concurrent commit changed.

methods.name: requireAdministrator
methods.comment: Giving the administrator role is what an administrator does; no other permission is enough.

methods.name: requireGrantable
methods.comment: Giving a role gives its permissions, so the giver must hold each of them, as when a role is edited ({@code RoleService}). Otherwise assigning roles would be a way to gain permissions, including by giving oneself a role. An administrator holds every permission and may give any role.

methods.name: requireUnscoped
methods.comment: A role with a scope type is assigned within a place, through the scoped-role endpoint; it cannot be given here, where it would have no place (Timetia ADR 0004).

methods.name: summaries
methods.comment: Built-in roles first, then by name.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.application.RoleChanges
comment: What an administrator supplies to change a role, with the version they started from so that an edit made meanwhile by someone else is not overwritten.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.application.RoleRetention
comment: Permanently removes roles that were deleted longer ago than the retention period (ADR 0034).

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.application.RoleService
comment: The use cases for roles (ADR 0025, ADR 0044). Every change is audited in its own transaction, and two rules stop role editing from becoming a way to escalate privilege: an editor can only give a role permissions they hold themselves, and the administrator role cannot be edited at all.

methods.name: permissions
methods.comment: Every permission the modules declare, for the role editor.

methods.name: withEffectivePermissions
methods.comment: The administrator role holds every declared permission without rows of its own, so the editor shows them all.

methods.name: requireGrantable
methods.comment: A role can only be given what its editor holds, or editing roles would be a way to gain permissions. A policy-decided permission is held through assignments in places, so no editor holds it as such: only an administrator may put one in a role (Timetia ADR 0004).

methods.name: validScopeType
methods.comment: An empty scope type means a platform role; otherwise it must be GLOBAL or a kind a module declared.

methods.name: requireConsistent
methods.comment: The two rules that keep scoped roles apart from platform roles (Timetia ADR 0004): a role that holds a policy-decided permission has a scope type, so it is never assigned without a place; and a role with a scope type holds only policy-decided permissions, so a flat permission is never held in a place that does not limit it.

methods.name: summarise
methods.comment: {@code +a,+b,-c}, or a count when that would not fit in an audit value.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.application.RoleStore
comment: Where roles, what they allow and who holds them are kept. The use cases depend on this port, never on JPA or SQL (ADR 0003). Everything acts on the current tenant. Taking a permission off a role and taking a role off a user delete the row; the audit log keeps the history (ADR 0050).

methods.name: insert
methods.comment: Creates a role. {@code scopeType} is null for a platform role (Timetia ADR 0004).

methods.name: findScopedByName
methods.comment: The live role with exactly this name, but only when it has a scope type: a platform role (the administrator, the user role, a custom one) is never found here, so what finds roles by name cannot hand one out (Timetia ADR 0006).

methods.name: update
methods.comment: Changes a role if it is still at {@code expectedVersion}, otherwise fails with an optimistic locking failure. A change to the permissions alone also advances the version.

methods.name: softDelete
methods.comment: Marks the role deleted. The caller has checked that nobody holds it.

methods.name: purgeDeletedBefore
methods.comment: Permanently removes roles deleted before the cutoff, with what they allowed. Returns how many.

methods.name: ensureBuiltInRoles
methods.comment: Creates the two built-in roles if they are missing and offers the user role any permission it has not seen.

methods.name: lock
methods.comment: Locks the role's row until the transaction ends, so concurrent changes to who holds it take turns.

methods.name: roleIdsOf
methods.comment: The platform roles the user holds: roles with no scope type. Roles with a scope type are in {@link #scopedAssignmentsOf}.

methods.name: scopedAssignmentsOf
methods.comment: The roles with a scope type that the user holds, one per role and place (Timetia ADR 0004).

methods.name: roleIdsOfAll
methods.comment: The role IDs of several users at once, without a place. A user who holds no role is absent from the map.

methods.name: holdersOf
methods.comment: The IDs of every user who holds the role, in any place.

methods.name: assign
methods.comment: Gives the role without a place.

methods.name: assign
methods.comment: Gives the role in a place; {@code scopeId} is null for the global scope.

methods.name: assignIfAbsent
methods.comment: Gives the role in a place unless the user already holds it there, and says whether it did. Two requests at the same moment give it once, and only one of them is told so; {@code scopeId} is null for the global scope.

methods.name: unassign
methods.comment: Takes the role away, without a place.

methods.name: unassign
methods.comment: Takes the role away in one place; {@code scopeId} is null for the global scope.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.application.RoleStore$ScopedAssignment
comment: A role held in a place; {@code scopeId} is null for a role whose scope type is GLOBAL.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.application.RoleTemplateService
comment: Creates the roles a module seeds at startup (Timetia ADR 0004), and leaves existing ones as they are.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.application.ScopedAssignmentService
comment:
Who holds which role in which place (Timetia ADR 0004). A role with a scope type carries policy-decided permissions; each assignment of it names the place it applies to, or none for {@code GLOBAL}.

The rules, each one a denial a test proves:

  • Only an administrator assigns such a role, because no editor holds a policy-decided permission as such. This is the administrative authorization of the scoped model: assignment power does not delegate in version 1 (Timetia ADR 0003).
  • The role must have a scope type. A platform role is assigned through {@link RoleAssignmentService}.
  • A {@code GLOBAL} role takes no place; every other scope type needs one, and the place must exist. With no {@link ScopeDirectory} to ask, a place cannot be validated, so it cannot be assigned (fail closed).
  • A place is named by its id or by its code, never both. Both are checked against the same directory.

The same rules serve the API (which sets the whole set of a user's scoped roles) and the provisioning import ({@link ScopedAssignments}, which only adds), so a file cannot do what the screen would refuse.

methods.name: scopedRolesOf
methods.comment: The roles a user holds in places, by role and place.

methods.name: replaceScopedRolesOfUser
methods.comment:
Makes the user's scoped roles exactly {@code wanted}. Every added and removed assignment is audited with the role, the scope type and the place; a repeated request changes nothing.

READ_COMMITTED like the other assignment changes, so what a concurrent commit changed is seen.

methods.name: addScopedRole
methods.comment: Gives the user one more scoped role and leaves the rest alone. Unlike {@link #replaceScopedRolesOfUser}, a screen that has not seen a newer change cannot overwrite it. Holding it already changes nothing and is not an error.

methods.name: removeScopedRole
methods.comment: Takes away one scoped role in one place, and says 404 when the user does not hold it there.

methods.name: validate
methods.comment: Checks every requested assignment and returns the set to hold. Collects the field errors of all of them.

methods.name: place
methods.comment: The one rule set for where a role applies. The place is named by {@code scopeId} or by {@code scopeCode} (a blank code is no code). Returns the place's id (null for a global role) or the rule it broke.

methods.name: refusal
methods.comment: 409 when places cannot be checked at all; otherwise 400 with the rule that was broken.

methods.name: requireAdministrator
methods.comment: A role that carries policy-decided permissions is given by an administrator: no one else holds those permissions as such, so no one else may give them (Timetia ADR 0004).

methods.name: codesOf
methods.comment: The codes of the places in the assignments, by kind, when something provides places; empty otherwise.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.application.ScopedAssignmentService$NewScopedRole
comment: One assignment a caller asks for. The place is {@code scopeId} or {@code scopeCode}, never both; both are null for a global role.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.application.ScopedAssignmentService$Place
comment: Where a role applies, or the rule that was broken.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.application.ScopedAssignmentService$ScopedRole
comment: A role assignment as it is shown: the role, its scope type and the place; {@code scopeId} is null for a global role, and {@code scopeCode} is null when there is no place or nothing provides the codes.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.domain.DefaultDecisionPoint
comment:
The Java policies behind the decision point (ADR 0027, ADR 0044, Timetia ADR 0004).

The rules, in order:

  1. The system may do anything. It is a caller created only by {@code Authorization#runAsSystem}.
  2. An action must be a registered permission; anything else is a programming error.
  3. A caller who has not verified their email address holds only the permissions marked {@code allowedBeforeVerification}.
  4. A policy-decided permission is never satisfied by the permission-only checks: they answer {@link Scope#NONE}. For one record it needs the caller to hold the permission through some assignment, a {@link ScopedResourcePolicy} that supports the record, and that policy's yes. With no such policy the answer is no.
  5. For any other permission, holding {@code -any} gives {@link Scope#ALL}. Holding {@code } gives {@link Scope#OWN} when the action has an {@code -any} variant, and {@link Scope#ALL} when it has none (an administrative action). Holding neither gives {@link Scope#NONE}.
  6. For one record: the record's tenant must be the caller's; a module's {@link ResourcePolicy} decides if there is one; otherwise {@code ALL} allows and {@code OWN} allows records the caller owns.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.domain.PermissionRegistry
comment: Every permission the modules declare in code (ADR 0044), collected at startup. The role editor lists from it and the decision point refuses permissions that are not in it, so a typo in {@code @RequiresPermission} is found at startup or on first use instead of silently denying forever.

methods.name: userRolePermissions
methods.comment: The permissions the built-in {@code user} role holds.

methods.name: isAllowedBeforeVerification
methods.comment: Whether a caller who has not verified their email address may use the permission (ADR 0041).

methods.name: isPolicyDecided
methods.comment: Whether the permission is decided per record from scoped grants (Timetia ADR 0004).

methods.name: hasAnyVariant
methods.comment: Whether the action has a {@code -any} variant, which makes the plain permission mean "records I own".

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.domain.PermissionSource
comment: Where a caller's permissions come from: the roles stored in the database, read by one indexed query per call so a change applies on the next request on any instance (ADR 0044).

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.domain.ScopeKinds
comment: The kinds of place a role can be assigned in (Timetia ADR 0004): {@code GLOBAL} and the kinds modules declare. A malformed name stops the application from starting.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.persistence.JpaRoleStore
comment: Keeps roles in MySQL. A role is a JPA entity, with the conventions of every business table. What it allows and who holds it are rows in link tables, written with SQL that names the tenant itself (ADR 0028): there is nothing in them worth a version or a soft delete, and the audit log is their history (ADR 0050).

methods.name: scopeOf
methods.comment: The place of a stored assignment: null for the all-zero id, which means no place.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.persistence.RoleEntity
comment: The table row of a role. Persistence only: it never leaves this package (ADR 0004). What the role allows and who holds it are in link tables the store reads with SQL, because they are plain rows with no history of their own.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.persistence.RoleRepository
comment: Entity queries are filtered by tenant and skip deleted roles on their own.

methods.name: lockById
methods.comment: {@code SELECT ... FOR UPDATE}: whoever holds the lock decides who may hold the role until the transaction ends.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.persistence.StoredPermissionSource
comment:
A caller's permissions from the roles stored in the database (ADR 0025, ADR 0044). Each call is one indexed query on the caller's assignments, so a role change, a removal or a disabled account applies on the very next request, on any number of application instances, with no cache to invalidate. The administrator role has no permission rows: it holds every flat permission the modules declare. Only roles without a scope type count here; a role that carries policy-decided permissions is read through {@link StoredScopedGrants}.

A stored permission that no module declares any more is ignored, so removing a module cannot leave a role pointing at something that does not exist.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.persistence.StoredScopedGrants
comment: Where a caller holds a policy-decided permission, from the stored role assignments (Timetia ADR 0004). Each call is one indexed query on the caller's assignments, so a change or a removal applies on the very next request on any instance, with no cache. Only live roles that carry a scope type count, and a deleted role grants nothing.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.web.AddScopedRoleRequest
comment: The body of {@code POST /api/v1/users/{id}/scoped-roles}: one more role for the user, in one place. It leaves every other assignment alone, so an administrator's screen that is out of date cannot undo what an import added. A role that applies everywhere takes neither field; every other names its place by {@code scopeId} or by {@code scopeCode}, never both.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.web.CreateRoleRequest
comment: The body of {@code POST /api/v1/roles}. The server validates; a client may check the same limits for usability. {@code scopeType} is left out for a platform role. A role that holds policy-decided permissions needs one, and a role with one holds only those (Timetia ADR 0004).

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.web.PermissionResponse
comment: A permission a module declares, as the role editor lists it.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.web.PermissionsController
comment: Every permission the modules declare in code, for the role editor (ADR 0044). The list is short and fixed for a running application, so it is not paged.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.web.ReplaceScopedRolesRequest
comment: The body of {@code PUT /api/v1/users/{id}/scoped-roles}: the roles the user should hold within scopes from now on. A role that applies everywhere takes no {@code scopeId}; every other needs one. This replaces the whole set, so a screen that may be out of date uses the one-assignment endpoints instead ({@link AddScopedRoleRequest}).

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.web.ReplaceScopedRolesRequest$ScopedRoleAssignmentRequest
comment: One role in one place.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.web.ReplaceUserRolesRequest
comment: The body of {@code PUT /api/v1/users/{id}/roles}: the roles the user should hold from now on.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.web.RoleMapper
comment: Converts between API types and application types by hand (ADR 0005).

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.web.RoleResponse
comment: A role as the API returns it. {@code version} is what a later update must send back. {@code builtIn} is null for a role an administrator created, and {@code ADMIN} or {@code USER} for the two the foundation protects; the administrator role's {@code permissions} lists every declared permission, because it holds them all.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.web.RoleSummaryResponse
comment: A role in a user's list of roles.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.web.RolesController
comment: Roles and what they allow (ADR 0025). The controller only converts and delegates; the use cases decide who may do what and write the audit entries.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.web.ScopedRoleResponse
comment: A role a user holds within a scope; {@code scopeId} is absent for a role that applies everywhere, and {@code scopeCode} is absent when there is no place or nothing provides the codes of places yet.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.web.ScopedUserRolesController
comment: The roles one user holds within scopes (Timetia ADR 0004). Putting the whole set keeps a retried request harmless; adding and removing one assignment is what a screen uses, so it never overwrites changes it has not seen. The roles without a scope are the ones behind {@code /api/v1/users/{id}/roles}.

methods.name: add
methods.comment: Adds one assignment (a repeat changes nothing) and returns everything the user now holds in places.

methods.name: remove
methods.comment: Removes one assignment and returns what remains; 404 when the user does not hold it.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.web.UpdateRoleRequest
comment: The body of {@code PUT /api/v1/roles/{id}}. {@code version} is the version the client last read: if the role changed since, the update is refused with 409 instead of overwriting the other change.

name: com.kibootia.backend.access.web.UserRolesController
comment: The roles one user holds (ADR 0025). Putting the whole set keeps a retried request harmless.

name: com.kibootia.backend.audit
comment: Audit module. See kibootia-docs/engineering/conventions/package-structure.md.

name: com.kibootia.backend.audit.AuditEntry
comment:
What a module asks the audit log to record (ADR 0046). People are referred to by user ID only: an entry never holds a name, an email address, a secret or a token, so erasing a user needs no rewrite of the append-only log. The actor, the time, the tenant and the trace ID are added by the log itself.

The constructor rejects the mistakes that would put personal data in the log: a change on a field named like personal data, and a value that looks like an email address. This is a guard against slips, not a substitute for choosing what to record.

methods.name: of
methods.comment: A successful action on a record.

methods.name: withChange
methods.comment: The same entry with one more changed field.

methods.name: failedWith
methods.comment: The same entry recorded as failed with the given code.

name: com.kibootia.backend.audit.AuditLog
comment:
The public API of the audit log (ADR 0046). Any module calls it from the use case that makes an auditable change.

The entry is written in the caller's transaction: a change cannot exist without its entry, and a rolled-back change leaves no entry. Calling it outside a transaction is an error, not a silent separate write.

methods.name: record
methods.comment: Records the entry for the current caller, tenant and trace. The actor is whoever is acting (the nil UUID for the system); it cannot be passed in, so a module cannot record an action on behalf of someone else.

name: com.kibootia.backend.audit.AuditPermissions
comment: The permissions of the audit module (ADR 0044). None is held by the built-in {@code user} role.

name: com.kibootia.backend.audit.application.AuditEntryStore
comment: Where audit entries are kept. The log is append-only: this port can add an entry, read entries and remove expired ones, and nothing else, so there is no update path to misuse (ADR 0046).

methods.name: search
methods.comment: A page of the caller's tenant's entries that match the filter, newest first unless the page says otherwise.

methods.name: deleteOccurredBefore
methods.comment: Removes the caller's tenant's entries that occurred before the cutoff and returns how many.

name: com.kibootia.backend.audit.application.AuditEntryStore$Entry
comment: An entry as written.

name: com.kibootia.backend.audit.application.AuditEntryStore$Filter
comment: What to look for; a null field matches everything.

name: com.kibootia.backend.audit.application.AuditEntryStore$Stored
comment: An entry as read back.

name: com.kibootia.backend.audit.application.AuditProperties
comment: Audit settings (ADR 0046).

name: com.kibootia.backend.audit.application.AuditRecord
comment: An audit entry as the viewer shows it: the stored entry plus the names of the people in it, looked up when it is shown and never stored (ADR 0046).

name: com.kibootia.backend.audit.application.AuditRecord$Person
comment: A person in an entry. Only the ID is stored, so a user who was erased can only be shown as erased.

name: com.kibootia.backend.audit.application.AuditService
comment: Writes audit entries and removes expired ones (ADR 0046).

methods.name: record
methods.comment: MANDATORY: the entry joins the transaction of the change it describes and fails loudly if there is none.

methods.name: purge
methods.comment: Removes the tenant's entries older than the retention period and returns how many.

name: com.kibootia.backend.audit.application.AuditViewer
comment: Shows the audit log to an administrator (ADR 0046). An entry holds only user IDs, so names are looked up here, when the entry is shown, through the {@code platform} user directory: a user's current name appears, and a user who was erased shows as erased, which pseudonymises the log without rewriting it.

name: com.kibootia.backend.audit.application.FailedEventService
comment: The view of events that keep failing, and the retry action (ADR 0031). The platform reads the registry; this module owns the administrative use case, so a retry is authorized and audited like every administrative change (ADR 0046). The platform's {@link FailedEvent} is the application model: it carries metadata only, never the event's payload.

methods.name: retry
methods.comment: Redelivers one failed event now. The audit entry is written first, in this transaction; the redelivery itself runs afterwards on another thread.

name: com.kibootia.backend.audit.application.SecurityEventRecorder
comment:
Records the refusals that the platform reports as audit entries (Timetia ADR 0005): a signed-in user refused a permission, a refused account, a rate-limit refusal. Each is written in its own transaction, because the refused request has none to join, and with the user ID, a permission name or a code only.

The number written for one user is limited per minute, so a flood of refused requests cannot fill the log. Reporting never changes the answer to the caller: a failure to write is logged and swallowed.

name: com.kibootia.backend.audit.persistence.AuditEntryEntity
comment: One audit entry as stored (ADR 0046). Immutable: Hibernate never updates it, and the repository offers no update. It carries the tenant but, deliberately, none of the soft-delete, version or audit columns of business tables: the log is append-only and is trimmed only by the retention purge (ADR 0034).

methods.name: requireTenant
methods.comment: A write needs a tenant; reads without one find nothing.

name: com.kibootia.backend.audit.persistence.AuditEntryMapper
comment: Converts the application's entry to the persistence entity by hand (ADR 0005).

name: com.kibootia.backend.audit.persistence.AuditEntryRepository
comment: Deliberately not a {@code JpaRepository}: the log accepts new entries and the retention purge, nothing else (ADR 0046). The tenant filter applies to the delete, so a purge only touches the caller's tenant.

methods.name: search
methods.signature: search(java.util.UUID, java.lang.String, java.lang.String, java.util.UUID, java.time.Instant, java.time.Instant, org.springframework.data.domain.Pageable)
methods.comment: The tenant filter applies, so only the caller's tenant's entries are found.

name: com.kibootia.backend.audit.persistence.JpaAuditEntryStore
comment: Keeps audit entries in MySQL.

methods.name: likePrefix
methods.comment: A LIKE pattern matching the start of an action code, with the caller's own % and _ made literal.

name: com.kibootia.backend.audit.web.AuditEntriesController
comment: The audit log for administrators (ADR 0046): read only, newest first. There is no way to change or delete an entry through the API; only the retention purge removes them.

name: com.kibootia.backend.audit.web.AuditEntryResponse
comment: An audit entry as the API returns it. People appear as an ID plus, when Kibootia still holds them, a name looked up now; the log itself stores only IDs (ADR 0046). The interface shows {@code ERASED} as "deleted user".

name: com.kibootia.backend.audit.web.FailedEventMapper
comment: Converts the application model to the API type by hand (ADR 0005).

name: com.kibootia.backend.audit.web.FailedEventResponse
comment: An event whose delivery failed, as the API shows it. Metadata only: the payload can hold personal data and is never returned.

name: com.kibootia.backend.audit.web.FailedEventsController
comment: Events that keep failing and their retry (ADR 0031). Administrators only; there is no screen yet.

methods.name: list
methods.comment: Oldest first. The order is fixed, so no sort field is accepted.

methods.name: retry
methods.comment: Redelivers the event. The delivery runs afterwards, so the answer is 202 Accepted.

name: com.kibootia.backend.files
comment: Files module. See kibootia-docs/engineering/conventions/package-structure.md.

name: com.kibootia.backend.files.FilesConfiguration
comment: Wires the files module (ADR 0024, ADR 0029): the S3 client, the default inspection hook and the creation of the bucket. With {@code kibootia.files.enabled=false} none of this exists.

methods.name: fileInspector
methods.comment: Accepts every upload; a deployment replaces it to scan for malware (a recipe, ADR 0029).

methods.name: bucketInitializer
methods.comment: Creates the bucket at startup when asked to. A storage server that is down must only affect file features (ADR 0047), so a failure is logged and the first upload tries again.

name: com.kibootia.backend.files.FilesPermissions
comment: The permissions of the files module (ADR 0044). Uploading and viewing a file are decided by the module that owns it, such as {@code identity} for an avatar, so the only permissions here are the two the jobs act with. No user holds them except through the administrator role; the jobs run as the system, which holds every permission.

name: com.kibootia.backend.files.application.ConditionalOnFilesEnabled
comment: Puts a bean of the {@code files} module in the application only while {@code kibootia.files.enabled} is not {@code false} (ADR 0024). With it off there is no storage client, no job and no listener, and the application starts without storage settings; the table stays migrated, so the schema checks still pass.

name: com.kibootia.backend.files.application.FileEvents
comment: What the files module does when something happens elsewhere (ADR 0031). The method is not public, so it is not a use case: it is reached only through the event, as the system, in the event's tenant, once per event even if the delivery repeats.

methods.name: on
methods.comment: A user was erased (ADR 0034): everything they stored goes at once, deleted files included, without waiting for the retention period. The objects first, then the rows; if the storage server is down the handler fails and is tried again, and deleting what is already gone is harmless.

name: com.kibootia.backend.files.application.FileInspector
comment: The hook where a deployment adds its own check of an upload, before anything is stored: a malware scanner such as ClamAV, or a rule about content (ADR 0029). The shipped implementation accepts everything; malware scanning is a recipe, not part of the foundation. Replace it by declaring another bean of this type.

methods.name: inspect
methods.comment: Throws an {@link com.kibootia.backend.platform.errors.ApiException} to refuse the upload, for example 422 with a code of its own. Returns normally to accept it.

name: com.kibootia.backend.files.application.FileRetention
comment: Removes files that were deleted longer ago than the retention period (ADR 0034): the stored objects first, then the rows. In that order, so a failure in between leaves rows that name objects that are gone, and the next run finishes the job; the other order would leave objects nothing refers to. Works in batches so one run is bounded.

name: com.kibootia.backend.files.application.FileService
comment:
Keeps files for the other modules (ADR 0029). The rules, in the order they are applied to an upload:
  1. the size limit, while reading, so an oversized upload is never held in memory;
  2. the type, found from the bytes. The filename and the declared content type are never looked at, because the sender chooses both;
  3. the inspection hook, where a deployment can add a malware scan;
  4. re-encoding: every rendition is a new image made from the pixels, so nothing hidden in the original survives.

The objects are written first and the metadata row last, each in its own short step, so no database transaction is ever open while the storage server is being called. A failure between the two leaves an object nothing refers to, which the reconciliation job removes once it is old enough to be sure no upload is still in progress.

Nothing here decides who may upload or see a file. The module that owns the file does, through the decision point.

methods.name: readAtMost
methods.comment: Reads the upload, refusing it as soon as it is larger than the limit.

methods.name: detectType
methods.comment: The type found from the first bytes, whatever the sender called the file.

name: com.kibootia.backend.files.application.FilesProperties
comment: Settings of the {@code files} module (ADR 0024, ADR 0029). The module is on by default; with {@code kibootia.files.enabled=false} none of its beans exist and the application starts without storage.

name: com.kibootia.backend.files.application.ImageProcessor
comment:
Turns an uploaded image into the renditions of its category (ADR 0029): decoded from the bytes, turned upright by its EXIF orientation, cut to the centred square or kept whole with its proportions (the rendition's shape), scaled to each size and written as a new PNG. A new image is drawn each time, so nothing of the original carries over: no EXIF, no GPS position, no embedded thumbnail, no comment, and nothing hidden after the end of the image. The original is never stored.

The decoder is told the size first and refuses an image with too many pixels, which is the usual way a small file grows into gigabytes of memory. A big image is read with subsampling, so it is never held at full size.

methods.name: exifOrientation
methods.comment: The EXIF orientation, 1 to 8, of a JPEG; 1 (as it is) for everything else and for a damaged EXIF block.

methods.name: orient
methods.comment: Turns an image upright from its EXIF orientation value (1 is already upright).

methods.name: fit
methods.comment: The whole image with its proportions, its longest side at most {@code longest}. An image that is already small enough keeps its size; it is still drawn anew, so nothing of the decoded original carries over.

methods.name: scale
methods.comment: Halves while the image is more than twice the target in both directions, then makes the last step, which keeps shrinking sharp. The result is always an image drawn here, never the one passed in.

name: com.kibootia.backend.files.application.ObjectStorage
comment:
The storage port of the {@code files} module (ADR 0029): the few operations the module needs from an S3-compatible server, with no vendor type in the signatures. The S3 adapter implements it; tests use an in-memory fake. Keys are built by the module ({@code ///}), never from user input.

Every method throws {@link Unavailable} when the server cannot be reached or refuses the call, so a storage outage is one failure the callers can turn into 503 and nothing else.

methods.name: ensureBucket
methods.comment: Creates the bucket when it does not exist. Safe to call again.

methods.name: get
methods.comment: The object, or empty when there is none. The caller closes the stream.

methods.name: delete
methods.comment: Deleting an object that is not there is not an error.

methods.name: deleteAll
methods.comment: Deletes up to a thousand keys at once; absent keys are ignored.

methods.name: list
methods.comment: One page of the objects whose key starts with the prefix, in key order.

methods.name: presignPut
methods.comment: A time-limited address the browser could upload to without the backend in between. No file category uses it yet; it exists because ADR 0029 makes presigned transfers an opt-in capability of the port.

methods.name: presignGet
methods.comment: A time-limited address the browser could download from. Also unused by any category yet.

methods.name: close
methods.comment: Releases the connection to the server; always close an object that was read.

name: com.kibootia.backend.files.application.ObjectStorage$Unavailable
comment: The server could not be reached, or refused the call. The message never carries a credential.

name: com.kibootia.backend.files.application.ReconciliationJob
comment:
Brings the object store and the metadata back in step (ADR 0029). Two things can drift: an upload that failed between writing its objects and its row leaves objects nothing refers to, and an object lost from the store leaves a row with nothing behind it.
  • An object whose file has no row is removed, once it is older than the grace period, so an upload that is still being written is never touched.
  • A row whose objects are missing is only reported. Metadata is never deleted on the word of a listing: a partial answer or an outage would otherwise erase the record of a file that is fine.

{@link ReconciliationSchedule} runs it daily under a database lock; it never holds a database transaction while the storage server is being called.

methods.name: runOnce
methods.comment: Reconciles every tenant now. A tenant that fails is logged and the others still run.

methods.name: countFilesMissingObjects
methods.comment: Rows older than the grace period whose file has no object in the listing. They are reported, never deleted.

methods.name: fileIdOf
methods.comment: The file ID in {@code <tenant>/<category>/<file>/<rendition>}, or null for a key that does not follow it.

name: com.kibootia.backend.files.application.ReconciliationJob$Result
comment: What a run found, for the logs and for tests.

name: com.kibootia.backend.files.application.ReconciliationSchedule
comment: Runs {@link ReconciliationJob} once a day (UTC, at {@code kibootia.files.reconcile-cron}). It takes a database lock, so with several instances one of them reconciles. Off, like every job, when {@code kibootia.jobs.enabled=false}.

name: com.kibootia.backend.files.application.StoredFileStore
comment: Where the metadata of stored files is kept (ADR 0003). Every method acts on the current tenant. {@link #find} sees live files only; the methods about deleted files and about erasure reach every row, because the retention job and the erasure of a user must.

methods.name: nextId
methods.comment: A new file ID, a UUIDv7 (ADR 0033). The ID is needed before the row exists, because the object keys contain it.

methods.name: find
methods.comment: A live file, or empty when there is none or it was deleted.

methods.name: softDelete
methods.comment: Marks a live file deleted. Returns false when there was none.

methods.name: findDeletedBefore
methods.comment: Files deleted before the cutoff, oldest first, at most {@code limit} of them.

methods.name: findByOwner
methods.comment: Every file of the owner, live or deleted.

methods.name: deleteAll
methods.comment: Removes the rows for good.

methods.name: existing
methods.comment: Which of these IDs have a row, live or deleted.

methods.name: idsCreatedBefore
methods.comment: The IDs of rows, live or deleted, created before the instant, in key order and after {@code after} (null for the first page). Reconciliation pages through these to find files whose objects are missing.

methods.name: tenantPrefix
methods.comment: The prefix every object of the tenant starts with.

name: com.kibootia.backend.files.persistence.JpaStoredFileStore
comment: Keeps file metadata in MySQL. A new row is a JPA entity with the conventions of every business table. What entity queries cannot see, deleted files, and what must reach every row, erasing an owner's files, is read and changed with SQL that names the tenant itself (ADR 0028, ADR 0034).

methods.name: insert
methods.comment: Its own short transaction: the storage server is never called while one is open.

methods.name: utc
methods.comment: DATETIME(6) columns hold UTC wall time, as Hibernate writes them.

name: com.kibootia.backend.files.persistence.StoredFileEntity
comment: The table row of a stored file. Persistence only: it never leaves this package (ADR 0004). The key is given, because the object keys contain it and the objects are written before the row; the tenant, version, audit columns and soft delete come from the platform base types.

name: com.kibootia.backend.files.s3.S3ObjectStorage
comment:
The {@link ObjectStorage} port on the standard AWS SDK for Java S3 client (ADR 0029). Any S3-compatible server works; changing server is a change of configuration. Path-style addressing is used because a local server has no wildcard DNS for bucket names.

The SDK's default is to add a trailing checksum to every upload and to validate one on every download. Servers that do not implement that reject the request, so both are set to "when required", which sends and checks a checksum only where the operation demands it.

methods.name: unavailable
methods.comment: The SDK's message can name the endpoint and request IDs but never a secret; the credentials are not part of it.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity
comment: Identity module. See kibootia-docs/engineering/conventions/package-structure.md.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.IdentityConfiguration
comment: Binds the {@code kibootia.identity.*} settings.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.IdentityPermissions
comment: The permissions of the identity module (ADR 0044, ADR 0041). None is held by the built-in {@code user} role: a new user sees no one else, because with open sign-up any stranger could otherwise browse the user directory. Actions on one's own profile need no permission; ownership allows them.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.UserErased
comment: Erasure of a user began: an administrator asked for it, or the retention period of a deleted user passed (ADR 0034). Part of the module's public contract. Other modules remove what they hold about the user through a {@code @DurableEventListener}, so the removal survives a restart. Identity itself deletes the Keycloak account and then the profile.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.AvatarService
comment:
The avatar of a user (ADR 0029, ADR 0041). The bytes are kept by the files module through the {@link StoredFiles} port, which this module asks for through an {@code ObjectProvider}: with the files module switched off the avatar endpoints answer 404 {@code files.disabled} and everything else works.

Who may do what:

  • A user changes only their own avatar, and only once their email address is verified, like any change to their own account. Uploads are rate limited.
  • A user always sees their own avatar, verified or not. Seeing anyone else's needs {@code identity.profiles.view}, the same permission as seeing their profile, and never crosses tenants.

The methods that change data are deliberately not one transaction: the storage server is called without a database transaction open, and only the switch of the profile's avatar is transactional (in the store).

methods.name: upload
methods.comment: Stores the upload as the caller's avatar, replacing the one they had. The replaced file is hidden at once and removed once its retention period has passed (ADR 0034).

methods.name: remove
methods.comment: Removes the caller's avatar. Does nothing when they have none.

methods.name: view
methods.comment: The avatar of a user, or what the caller already has. A user with no avatar, an unknown user, a deleted user and a user of another tenant all give empty, so a caller who may look learns nothing from the difference.

methods.name: matches
methods.comment: Whether an {@code If-None-Match} header names this entity tag; weak tags and {@code *} count.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.AvatarService$Image
comment: The avatar as PNG bytes. The caller streams it and closes it.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.AvatarService$NotModified
comment: The caller's copy is current; nothing is sent.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.AvatarService$View
comment: The answer to a request for an avatar.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.AvatarSize
comment: The sizes an avatar is kept in. The names are the renditions of {@link AvatarService#AVATAR}.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.BootstrapAdministratorInvitation
comment:
Gets a fresh environment its first Super Admin without anyone touching the database or the identity provider's console (Timetia ADR 0006, work package W3.3).

At startup, when {@code kibootia.identity.bootstrap-admin-email} is set and nobody holds the administrator role, the account for that address is created and invited exactly as an invitation would be. The person is made administrator when they follow the link and sign in for the first time ({@link ProfileGate}), and only while there is still no administrator. Once one exists this does nothing, whatever the setting says.

It is safe to repeat. Restarting after the account exists changes nothing, with one exception: if the person has still not signed in (for example the link expired) and there is still no administrator, the invitation is sent again, so a stuck environment can be recovered with a restart and no database work.

If the identity provider cannot be reached the application still starts: the next start tries again. An address the identity provider already knows (the local demo administrator, an account made by hand) is left alone, and that person becomes administrator at their first sign-in through the same rule.

Turned off by {@code kibootia.identity.bootstrap-invite.enabled=false}, which the integration tests use.

methods.name: invite
methods.comment: Does the work of {@link #run}; public so a test can start it again as a restart would.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.EmailAddresses
comment: The one rule for what counts as an email address and how it is compared, so an invitation, an import and a lookup agree on who is the same person. Deliberately simple: Keycloak has the final say, and the address is only used to find the account.

methods.name: normalize
methods.comment: The address stripped and lower-cased, or empty when it is not shaped like an email address.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.ErasureStarter
comment: The first step of erasing a user, shared by an administrator's request and the retention job: record that it began, audit it and publish the event the durable handlers react to. It runs in the caller's transaction. It carries no transaction or security annotation of its own, so it is a plain object, not a proxy: the caller has already authorized the erasure.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.IdentityProperties
comment: The identity module's settings (ADR 0025, ADR 0041).

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.IdentityProviderAdmin
comment:
What Kibootia asks of Keycloak to manage the user lifecycle (ADR 0025): the port in front of the Admin API. Only the adapter in the {@code keycloak} package knows it is Keycloak, so another identity provider can replace it, though the sign-in flow still assumes OpenID Connect.

Every method may throw {@link Unavailable} when the provider cannot be reached or refuses the call. The use cases answer that with 503; the durable event handlers let it propagate, so the retry policy tries again.

methods.name: createUser
methods.comment: Creates the account.  @throws EmailInUse when an account with this email address exists

methods.name: find
methods.comment: The account, or empty when the provider does not know it.

methods.name: setEnabled
methods.comment: Disables or enables the account. Disabling also ends the user's sessions.

methods.name: endSessions
methods.comment: Ends every session of the user, so their tokens stop being refreshed.

methods.name: sendInvitation
methods.comment: Emails the user a link to set a password; Keycloak sends it.

methods.name: sendVerificationEmail
methods.comment: Emails the user a link to verify their address; Keycloak sends it.

methods.name: delete
methods.comment: Deletes the account. Does nothing when it is already gone.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.IdentityProviderAdmin$Account
comment: What the provider holds about an account that Kibootia needs to know.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.IdentityProviderAdmin$EmailInUse
comment: An account with the email address exists.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.IdentityProviderAdmin$Unavailable
comment: The provider could not be reached or refused the call. The message must not contain secrets.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.ImportCsv
comment:
Reads the provisioning import file (Timetia ADR 0006): UTF-8 text, comma separated, one assignment per row, with a header naming the columns {@code email}, {@code role} and {@code scope} in any order ({@code scope} may be left out when no row needs one). A strict subset of RFC 4180: a field may be quoted, a quote inside it is doubled, a quoted field may span lines, rows end with LF or CRLF, a UTF-8 byte order mark is ignored, and blank lines are skipped.

The file as a whole is refused, with a message, when it cannot be read at all: bad encoding, a quote that is never closed or is in the wrong place, a header that is missing or wrong, no rows, or too many. A single bad row is not a reason to refuse the file: it comes back as a {@link Row} with a problem, and the import reports it.

Nothing here looks at what the cells mean. That is the import's job.

methods.name: parse
methods.comment: Parses the file, or throws a 400 (or 413 for too many rows) describing why it cannot be read at all.

methods.name: tokenize
methods.comment: Splits the text into records of fields. Blank lines are dropped.

methods.name: isBlank
methods.comment: A record that is a single empty value: a line with nothing (or only spaces) on it.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.ImportCsv$CsvRecord
comment: The fields of one record and the line it starts on.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.ImportCsv$Row
comment: One data row. {@code line} is the line in the file where the row starts (the header is line 1). When {@code problemCode} is set the row cannot be used and the cells may be empty.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.Invitation
comment: What an administrator supplies to invite someone: an email address and, optionally, roles to give them besides the built-in user role. Naming roles needs the permission to assign roles.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.MyProfile
comment: The signed-in user as {@code GET /api/v1/me} shows them. {@code emailVerified} is the token's word, not the stored copy's, because the decision point enforces verification from the token (ADR 0041). {@code permissions} is for the interface to decide what to show; the backend enforces every check itself, and a user who has not verified their address holds none. {@code avatarsEnabled} says whether the files module is running, so the interface shows the avatar controls only where they can work. {@code filesEnabled} says the same thing for every other feature that keeps files (a note's picture), so those features need not borrow the name of the avatar's flag. {@code administrator} says the user holds the built-in administrator role (Timetia's Super Admin) with a verified address; the interface shows the controls only an administrator can use, and the backend still refuses anyone else.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.ProfileGate
comment:
Runs before every authenticated API request (ADR 0041). It is the one place that turns "a valid token" into "a user Kibootia knows":
  • a user seen for the first time gets a profile, the built-in {@code user} role and, when their verified email address is the bootstrap one and nobody is an administrator yet, the administrator role;
  • a user already known has name and email refreshed from the token, once per token;
  • a user who was disabled or deleted is refused with 403, from the very next request, whatever their token says.

A user it has not seen is first checked against Keycloak. Without that, an old token of a user who was just erased would create the profile again.

methods.name: grantBootstrapAdministrator
methods.comment: In the caller's transaction. Does nothing once an administrator exists.

methods.name: isBootstrapAdministrator
methods.comment: The setting names an address; the token must carry it, verified, so registering with it first proves nothing.

methods.name: refresh
methods.comment: Copies the token's facts into the profile when the token is newer; a lost race is retried by the next request.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.ProfileService
comment: What a signed-in user does with their own account (ADR 0041). These need no permission: ownership is the rule, so every active user may do them. Viewing one's own profile and asking for the verification email again also work before the email address is verified; changing preferences does not.

methods.name: resendVerificationEmail
methods.comment: Asks Keycloak to send the verification email again. Rate limited, because each call sends a mail. A user whose address is already verified is told so, which usually means their token is simply out of date.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.UserAccountChanged
comment: A user was disabled, enabled, deleted or restored. The handler brings the Keycloak account in line with the profile as it is when the handler runs, so a repeated or late delivery is harmless.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.UserAdministration
comment:
What an administrator does with other people's accounts (ADR 0041). Each change is authorized, rate limited, audited and written in one transaction with the event that brings Keycloak in line, so Kibootia refuses a disabled or deleted user from the next request while Keycloak catches up through the durable event, with retries.

Two safeguards: nobody can change their own account here (an administrator who disables themselves has locked themselves out), and the last administrator who can still sign in cannot be disabled or deleted. Those that can remove an administrator run at {@code READ_COMMITTED} so the count behind the second safeguard sees what a concurrent commit changed.

methods.name: invite
methods.comment: Creates the account in Keycloak, then Kibootia's profile, roles, audit entry and the event that sends the mail. The account comes first because its ID is the profile's key. If Kibootia's part fails, the account is removed again, so a failed invitation leaves nothing behind. The address is marked verified: the link in the email proves the mailbox when the user follows it.

methods.name: inviteForImport
methods.comment: An invitation made by the provisioning import (Timetia ADR 0006): exactly like {@link #invite}, so the account, the profile, the default role, the audit entry and the mail are the same, but with {@code inSameTransaction} run with the new user's ID before the transaction commits. If it throws, the account is removed again. Not limited by the invitation rate limit: the import has its own. Package-private on purpose: only {@link UserImportService}, which has checked that the caller is an administrator, may call it, and no other module can.

methods.name: inviteBootstrapAdministrator
methods.comment: Invites the bootstrap administrator when the application starts, with no user to authorize it (Timetia ADR 0006). Only {@link BootstrapAdministratorInvitation}, which has checked the setting and that nobody is an administrator, calls it.

methods.name: resendBootstrapInvitation
methods.comment: Sends a bootstrap administrator's invitation again, at startup, when they have still not accepted it.

methods.name: resendInvitation
methods.comment: Sends the invitation again to a user who has not accepted it.

methods.name: erase
methods.comment: Begins erasing a deleted user, on a privacy request: Keycloak's account, the profile, the roles and what other modules hold are removed by durable handlers, which retry until they succeed. The audit log keeps only the user's ID, which shows as "deleted user" from then on.

methods.name: createInvitedUser
methods.comment: The one way an invited account is made, shared by an invitation and by the import: the identity provider's account, then in one transaction the profile, the default role, whatever {@code more} adds, the audit entry and the event that sends the mail. {@code audit} builds the entry, so each way in is told apart in the log.

methods.name: live
methods.comment: The profile, unless it is deleted: most actions do not apply to a deleted user, who looks absent to them.

methods.name: requireMayActOn
methods.comment: Only an administrator may disable, enable, delete, restore or erase an administrator's account. The permission to do so to ordinary users is not enough to lock out someone who holds every permission.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.UserDetails
comment: A user as an administrator sees them: the profile and the roles the user holds.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.UserEvents
comment:
The reactions to what happens to a user (ADR 0031, ADR 0041): everything that must reach Keycloak. They are durable handlers, so Keycloak being down delays them instead of losing them, and each is written to be run again with the same effect, because delivery is at least once.

The methods are not public, so they are not use cases: they are reached only through the event, as the system, in the event's tenant.

methods.name: on
methods.comment: An invitation, or a repeated one: Keycloak emails the set-password link.

methods.name: on
methods.comment: A user registered without a verified address: Keycloak sends the verification mail.

methods.name: on
methods.comment: Brings the Keycloak account in line with the profile as it is now, whatever happened in between: enabled only for a user who is neither disabled nor deleted. A user who should not sign in also has their sessions ended, every time, so a repeated delivery cannot leave one open.

methods.name: on
methods.comment: Erases the user: the Keycloak account first, then the profile and the roles. In that order, so that until the account is gone the profile still refuses the user; a failure after the first step is retried and deleting an account that is gone is harmless. The audit log keeps the user's ID only.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.UserImportProperties
comment: The limits of the provisioning import (Timetia ADR 0006). They keep one request from running for minutes or sending an unbounded number of emails; a file that is too big is split, and because a repeated import only adds, running the same file again is always safe.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.UserImportReport
comment: What an import did, or for a dry run what it would do, line by line in the order of the file (Timetia ADR 0006). It is handed back to the administrator who uploaded the file and is never logged or audited: it contains the addresses.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.UserImportReport$Line
comment: One row of the file. {@code email}, {@code role} and {@code scope} are as written (the email is the normalised form when it could be read). {@code userId} is the person's ID when there is one; {@code accountCreated} says this row's person got their account from this import.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.UserImportReport$Outcome
comment: What happened to a row.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.UserImportService
comment:
Loads people and their scoped roles from a file (Timetia ADR 0006, work package W3.1).

What it guarantees, each backed by a test:

  • Administrators only. The caller must be the built-in Administrator (Super Admin), whatever other permissions they hold. The same rule as assigning a scoped role through the screen.
  • Only roles that apply within a scope. A file cannot name the Administrator role, the user role or a custom platform role, so an import can never make anyone an administrator. Every row goes through the same checks as the screen ({@link ScopedAssignments}).
  • Add only. It creates missing accounts and adds missing assignments. It never removes or changes anything, and it never touches a disabled or deleted person. Running the same file again changes nothing.
  • A person's rows go together or not at all. If any row of a person has an error, none of theirs is applied, so no account is created from half a mistake. The other people are not affected.
  • No half-made people. A new person's account, profile, roles and audit entries are one transaction; if it fails the identity provider's account is removed again.
  • A dry run writes nothing and does not contact the identity provider. It shows what the same file would do, except that it cannot know an address the identity provider already has without a profile here.
  • Bounded. A size and row limit, a time budget, a stop after repeated identity provider failures, a rate limit, and one real import at a time.

The report goes back to the administrator and nowhere else: it holds the addresses, which are never logged or put in the audit log. The audit log gets one summary entry per real run, with counts only, plus the entries the invitation and each added assignment write.

methods.name: run
methods.comment: Runs the import. Not one transaction: each person is their own, so a failure affects only that person and what was done before it stays.

methods.name: resolve
methods.comment: Turns each usable row's role and place names into a role and a place, with the same checks as the screen.

methods.name: applyPerson
methods.comment: Applies one person's rows. Returns whether it failed because the identity provider could not be reached.

methods.name: record
methods.comment: One audit entry for the run, with counts only. The people and assignments have their own entries.

methods.name: exclusively
methods.comment: One real import at a time per tenant, across application instances.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.UserImportService$Entry
comment: A row while it is being processed.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.UserInvited
comment: An invited user's account exists in Keycloak; the handler asks Keycloak to email the set-password link. A durable event, so a Keycloak outage delays the mail instead of losing it.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.UserProfile
comment: A user's profile as the use cases see it, apart from the table row and the API type (ADR 0004). Keycloak is the source of truth for username, email and name; this is a read copy, refreshed from the token and never edited here (ADR 0041). What Kibootia owns is the status, the roles (in {@code access}) and the preferences.

methods.name: displayName
methods.comment: The name to show: first and last name, else the username. Never an email address (ADR 0046).

methods.name: canSignIn
methods.comment: Whether the user can use the application right now.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.UserProfile$Status
comment: Whether the user may sign in. A deleted user is not shown as disabled; deletion is a separate fact.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.UserProfile$Theme
comment: The colour scheme the user prefers.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.UserProfileStore
comment: Where user profiles are kept. The use cases depend on this port, never on JPA or SQL (ADR 0003). Every method acts on the current tenant. Unlike most stores, {@link #find} and {@link #search} can see soft-deleted profiles: an administrator restores or erases a deleted user, and the request gate must tell a deleted user from a new one.

methods.name: find
methods.comment: The profile, including a deleted one.

methods.name: insert
methods.comment: Creates the profile and flushes, so a profile created at the same moment by another request is reported by this call as a {@link org.springframework.dao.DataIntegrityViolationException} instead of at commit.

methods.name: refresh
methods.comment: Copies what the token says into the profile, once per token: only when the token is newer than the last copy and something differs. An invited user becomes active on the first sign-in.

methods.name: replaceAvatar
methods.comment: Makes the file the user's avatar, or removes the avatar when {@code fileId} is null, and returns the avatar the user had before (null when there was none). It holds a lock on the profile for the change, so two uploads at the same moment leave exactly one avatar and each hands back the one it replaced, which the caller then discards.

methods.name: softDelete
methods.comment: Marks a live profile deleted. It stays until it is erased.

methods.name: restore
methods.comment: Brings a deleted profile back. Returns false when there is no deleted profile that erasure has not begun on.

methods.name: markErasureRequested
methods.comment: Records that erasure began, so the retention job does not start it again.

methods.name: erase
methods.comment: Removes the row for good.

methods.name: search
methods.comment: A page of profiles matching the filter, deleted ones only when the filter asks for them.

methods.name: findExpiredDeleted
methods.comment: Deleted profiles whose retention period has passed and whose erasure has not begun.

methods.name: findByEmail
methods.comment: Every profile, deleted ones too, that has this email address, ignoring case. Normally at most one; the column is not unique, so a caller that needs one person must treat more than one as ambiguous.

methods.name: findByEmails
methods.comment: The same for many addresses at once, for the import: the profiles by lower-cased address. An address nobody has is absent from the map. The addresses must already be lower-cased.

methods.name: emailInUse
methods.comment: Whether a profile, deleted or not, already has this email address.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.UserProfileStore$NewProfile
comment: What a new profile is created from.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.UserProfileStore$TokenFacts
comment: What the token tells about the user, copied into the profile.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.UserRetention
comment: Starts erasing users who were deleted longer ago than the retention period (ADR 0034). It only begins the erasure, exactly as an administrator's request does: the Keycloak account, the profile and what other modules hold are removed by durable handlers that retry until they succeed. A user whose erasure has begun is not picked again.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.application.VerificationEmailRequested
comment: A user signed up and their email address is not verified; the handler asks Keycloak to send the verification mail. Keycloak's own setting that does this on registration is off, because Kibootia enforces verification itself (ADR 0041).

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.keycloak.KeycloakAdminAdapter
comment:
Talks to the Keycloak Admin API with a service-account client that holds only the realm-management roles it needs, never realm-admin (ADR 0025, ADR 0045). It is the only class that knows the provider is Keycloak.

The access token is fetched on first use and kept until shortly before it expires; a 401 from the Admin API drops it and tries once more. A failure of any kind is reported as {@link IdentityProviderAdmin.Unavailable} with a message that never contains the secret, a token or a response body, which can echo personal data.

methods.name: setEnabled
methods.comment: Reads the whole account, changes the flag and writes it back, as Keycloak's own console does. A partial update could clear attributes of an account that uses the user profile feature.

methods.name: returnAddress
methods.comment: The web application's front door: the one place a link in an email may send the user back to.

methods.name: authorized
methods.comment: Runs a call with a bearer token. A 401 means the cached token was refused, so a fresh one is fetched and the call is made once more. Anything else that goes wrong becomes {@link Unavailable}, except the client errors the callers handle themselves (404, 409), which pass through as they are.

name: com.kibootia.backend.identity.persistence.JpaUserDirectory
comment: Answers other modules' questions about users (ADR 0039) from the profile table. It reads deleted profiles too, so an administrator who deleted a user still sees their name in the audit log until the user is erased; after that the row is gone and the viewer shows "deleted user".
